newsitem.title: USA: Gene that may cause prostate cancer found.
newsitem.headline: Gene that may cause prostate cancer found.

text.p: Researchers have found the first proof that prostate cancer runs in families, locating a gene that increases the likelihood of developing the disease.
The finding to be published in Friday's edition of the journal "Science" is expected to shed light on how prostate cancer develops and perhaps on how to prevent and treat it, the researchers said.

Researchers at the National Center for Human Genome Research at Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore and Umea University in Sweden reported on a study involving 91 familes in which at least three members suffered from prostate cancer.

The gene they discovered, called HPC-1 for hereditary prostate cancer, is situated on the long arm of the chromosome, they said, and alterations to it account for at least a third of familial prostate cancer. They said testing for genetic susceptibility and for the presence of the HPC-1 gene could lead to early detection and prevent deaths.

In the United States, men stand a one-in-five chance of developing the cancer, the most common among men and the cause of more than 40,000 deaths a year. Researchers suspect that high-fat diets, multiple sex partners and cigarette smoking may heighten the risk, but the evidence is not conclusive.
Familial or hereditary prostate cancer accounts for about one in 10 cases, the researchers said.

"We know this gene seems to contribute to prostate cancer risk in a number of ethnic backgrounds," said Dr. Jeffrey Trent, head of the Johns Hopkins laboratory where the research took place. "There's linkage in Swedish families as well as American families including African American families."
Prostate cancer varies widely among ethnic groups with African American men suffering the highest rate in the world, 180 per 100,000, and the highest death rate, 54 per 100,000.
Among white American males the rate is about 135 per 100,000. For Hispanic and Japanese American men it is about 89 per 100,000 and it is still lower for other Asian Americans.
About 317,000 men in the United States will be diagnosed with prostate cancer this year.
